claim: Chi3l1 expression is substantially increased in SPF mice compared to germ-free mice in intestinal tissue.
source: We observed a substantial increase of Chi3l1 expression in SPF mice compared to germ-free mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical staining data shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Chi3l1 is primarily expressed in enteroendocrine cells in the ileum.
source: Our results revealed that Chi3l1 is primarily expressed in enteroendocrine cells in the ileum and goblet or Paneth cells in the colon (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-staining experiments with cell-type specific markers shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Chi3l1 is primarily expressed in goblet or Paneth cells in the colon.
source: Our results revealed that Chi3l1 is primarily expressed in enteroendocrine cells in the ileum and goblet or Paneth cells in the colon (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-staining experiments with cell-type specific markers shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Chi3l1 expression was not observed in tuft cells.
source: However, Chi3l1 expression was not observed in tuft cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-staining data with DCLK1, a tuft cell marker, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bacterial extract from wildtype mouse feces directly induces Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells.
source: We found that the bacterial extract directly induced Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C after treating DLD-1 cells with bacterial extract.

claim: E. coli specifically stimulates Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells.
source: Our results revealed that E. coli specifically stimulated Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells, while Staphylococcus sciuri did not have the same effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis comparing E. coli and S. sciuri treatment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Staphylococcus sciuri does not stimulate Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells.
source: Our results revealed that E. coli specifically stimulated Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells, while Staphylococcus sciuri did not have the same effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis comparing E. coli and S. sciuri treatment shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Heat-killed E. coli induces Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells.
source: We found that treatment of DLD-1 cells with heat-killed E. coli also led to an induction of Chi3l1 expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 1E after treating DLD-1 cells with heat-killed E. coli.

claim: The induction of Chi3l1 expression does not necessarily require live bacteria.
source: These findings suggest that the induction of Chi3l1 expression does not necessarily require live bacteria and that bacterial components alone are sufficient to induce this response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that heat-killed E. coli can induce Chi3l1 expression.

claim: LPS successfully induces Chi3l1 expression in DLD-1 cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, LPS successfully induced Chi3l1 expression (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Chitin and peptidoglycan have similar structures.
source: By comparing the structure of chitin with that of PGN, a component of bacterial cell walls, we observed that they have similar structures (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both chitin and PGN contain N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and have β–1,4-glycosidic bonds in their structures.
source: Both chitin and PGN contain N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and have β–1,4-glycosidic bonds in their structures.
evidence: The claim is stated in the caption of Figure 2A describing the structural comparison.

claim: rmChi3l1 can directly interact with Gram-positive bacteria.
source: We found that rmChi3l1 was present in the pellet obtained from both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (Figure 2B), suggesting that Chi3l1 can directly interact with bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-incubation and precipitation experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: rmChi3l1 can directly interact with Gram-negative bacteria.
source: We found that rmChi3l1 was present in the pellet obtained from both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (Figure 2B), suggesting that Chi3l1 can directly interact with bacteria.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-incubation and precipitation experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: rmChi3l1 interacts with PGN.
source: Consistent with our previous results, we observed that rmChi3l1 was present in the pellet obtained from PGN but not in the pellet obtained from bovine serum albumin (BSA), which served as a negative control (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-incubation and precipitation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: rhChi3l1 interacts with PGN.
source: Furthermore, we also examined the interaction between PGN and recombinant human Chi3l1 (rhChi3l1) and obtained similar results (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-incubation and precipitation experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Chi3l1 interacts with bacteria through PGN.
source: These findings indicate that Chi3l1 interacts with bacteria through PGN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Chi3l1 binds to both bacteria and PGN.

claim: Chi3l1 interacts with PGN in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Our results indicate that Chi3l1 interacts with PGN in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The binding between Chi3l1 and chitin does not exhibit dose dependency.
source: In contrast, the binding between Chi3l1 and chitin did not exhibit dose dependency (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The adhesion ability of the GlmM mutant (PGN synthesis-deficient) to DLD-1 cells significantly decreased.
source: The results showed that the adhesion ability of the GlmM mutant to cells significantly decreased (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial adhesion assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Knocking down Chi3l1 in DLD-1 cells decreases bacterial adhesion.
source: Additionally, after knocking down Chi3l1 in DLD-1 cells (knockdown efficiency over 50%), we observed a decrease in bacterial adhesion (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by bacterial adhesion assay data after Chi3l1 knockdown shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The Chi3l1-PGN interaction plays a crucial role in bacterial adhesion.
source: These findings suggest that the Chi3l1-PGN interaction plays a crucial role in bacterial adhesion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observations that PGN-deficient mutants and Chi3l1 knockdown both reduce bacterial adhesion.

claim: The bacterial population is relatively lower in IECΔChil1 littermates compared to Villin-cre littermates.
source: Our analysis of alpha diversity revealed that the bacterial population was relatively lower in IECΔChil1 littermates compared to Villin-cre littermates (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by alpha diversity analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: IECΔChil1 mice show lower bacterial enrichment in feces and ileum contents compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: This finding was further confirmed by conducting universal bacterial 16S rRNA qPCR analysis of the feces and ileum contents of IECΔChil1 and Villin-cre littermates, which also showed lower bacterial enrichment in IECΔChil1 mice (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There are significant differences in bacterial diversity between Villin-cre and IECΔChil1 littermates.
source: Furthermore, principal component analysis demonstrated significant differences in bacterial diversity between Villin-cre and IECΔChil1 littermates (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Gram-positive bacteria are significantly reduced in IECΔChil1 mice compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: When we examined the relative abundance of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria between Villin-cre and IECΔChil1 littermates, we observed that Gram-positive bacteria were significantly reduced in IECΔChil1 mice, while there was no notable difference in Gram-negative bacteria (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is no notable difference in Gram-negative bacteria between IECΔChil1 and Villin-cre mice.
source: When we examined the relative abundance of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria between Villin-cre and IECΔChil1 littermates, we observed that Gram-positive bacteria were significantly reduced in IECΔChil1 mice, while there was no notable difference in Gram-negative bacteria (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IECΔChil1 mice have lower abundance of Gram-positive bacteria compared to Villin-cre mice as shown by LTA staining.
source: This result was further validated by staining lipoteichoic acid (LTA), a component present on Gram-positive bacteria, which revealed a lower abundance of Gram-positive bacteria in IECΔChil1 compared to Villin-cre littermates (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining of LTA shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Firmicutes levels are reduced in the colon lumen of IECΔChil1 mice compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: Moreover, visualization of Firmicutes by bacteria fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) staining, a dominant group of Gram-positive bacteria in the gut, also showed reduced levels of Firmicutes in the colon lumen of IECΔChil1 mice compared to Villin-cre mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH staining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Lactobacillus is significantly reduced in IECΔChil1 mice compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: Analysis of the relative abundance of specific Gram-positive bacterial species demonstrated a significant reduction in Lactobacillus in IECΔChil1 mice compared to Villin-cre mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Similar reductions in Lactobacillus were observed in Chil1-/- mice compared to wildtype mice.
source: Similar results were observed in Chil1-/- mice compared to wildtype mice (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by 16S rRNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Turicibacter is more abundant in IECΔChil1 mice than Villin-cre mice.
source: Consist with the 16S rRNA sequencing analysis data, qPCR results showed that Turicibacter was more abundant in IECΔChil1 mice than Villin-cre mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Chi3l1 plays a role in regulating the colonization of Gram-positive bacteria, particularly Lactobacillus, in the murine gut.
source: These findings suggest that Chi3l1 plays a role in regulating the colonization of Gram-positive bacteria, particularly Lactobacillus, in the murine gut.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Chi3l1 deficiency leads to reduced Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus.

claim: Mouse Chi3l1 is specifically expressed in intestinal secretory epithelial cells and secreted into the intestinal lumen.
source: These findings indicate that mouse Chi3l1 is specifically expressed in intestinal secretory epithelial cells and secreted into the intestinal lumen.
evidence: The claim is inferred from immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence data showing Chi3l1 in secretory cells and mucus layer.

claim: A large amount of Chi3l1 signals are present in the mucus layer of the colon.
source: Immunohistochemistry staining of Chi3l1 in the colon revealed a large amount of Chi3l1 signals in the mucus layer (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry staining shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Chi3l1 is detected in the ileum and colonic tissues and mucus layer.
source: Furthermore, Chi3l1 was also detected in the ileum and colonic tissues and mucus layer (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The ileum mucus of Chil1-/- mice has significantly lower levels of Gram-positive bacteria compared to wildtype mice.
source: Quantification of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus using qPCR revealed that both the ileum and colon mucus of Chil1-/- mice had significantly lower levels of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus compared to that of wildtype mice (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The colon mucus of Chil1-/- mice has significantly lower levels of Gram-positive bacteria compared to wildtype mice.
source: Quantification of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus using qPCR revealed that both the ileum and colon mucus of Chil1-/- mice had significantly lower levels of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus compared to that of wildtype mice (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The ileum mucus of Chil1-/- mice has significantly lower levels of Lactobacillus compared to wildtype mice.
source: Quantification of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus using qPCR revealed that both the ileum and colon mucus of Chil1-/- mice had significantly lower levels of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus compared to that of wildtype mice (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The colon mucus of Chil1-/- mice has significantly lower levels of Lactobacillus compared to wildtype mice.
source: Quantification of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus using qPCR revealed that both the ileum and colon mucus of Chil1-/- mice had significantly lower levels of Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus compared to that of wildtype mice (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Chil1-/- mice have much lower colonization of E. faecalis compared to wildtype mice.
source: The data demonstrated that Chil1-/- mice had much lower colonization of E. faecalis compared to wildtype mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by rectal injection experiments with FDAA-labeled E. faecalis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Chil1-/- mice have much higher colonization of E. coli compared to wildtype mice.
source: Besides Gram-positive bacteria, we also performed rectal injection of both wildtype and Chil1-/- mice with mCherry-OP50 (a strain of E. coli that expresses mCherry), we found Chil1-/- mice had much higher colonization of E. coli compared to wildtype mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by rectal injection experiments with mCherry-OP50 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Chi3l1 promotes the colonization of Gram-positive bacteria, particularly Lactobacillus, in the intestinal mucus.
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that Chi3l1 promotes the colonization of Gram-positive bacteria, particularly Lactobacillus, in the intestinal mucus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing reduced Gram-positive bacteria and Lactobacillus in Chi3l1-deficient mice.

claim: The deletion of Chi3l1 significantly reduces mucus layer thickness.
source: Additionally, we also observed that the deletion of Chi3l1 significantly reduced mucus layer thickness, which may be attributed to the disrupted colonization of Gram-positive bacteria in the intestinal mucus layer (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by AB-PAS staining and Mucin 2 immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: There is a significant increase in Chil1 mRNA expression in the colon tissues of patients with CD compared to normal tissues.
source: We observed a significant increase in Chil1 mRNA expression in the colon tissues of patients with either CD or UC compared to normal tissues (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of GEO datasets shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a significant increase in Chil1 mRNA expression in the colon tissues of patients with UC compared to normal tissues.
source: We observed a significant increase in Chil1 mRNA expression in the colon tissues of patients with either CD or UC compared to normal tissues (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of GEO datasets shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Without DSS challenge, the colon length is similar between Villin-cre and IEC∆Chil1 mice.
source: Without the DSS challenge, the colon length and structure were similar between Villin-cre and IEC∆Chil1 mice (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by colon length measurements and H&E staining shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Without DSS challenge, the colon structure is similar between Villin-cre and IEC∆Chil1 mice.
source: Without the DSS challenge, the colon length and structure were similar between Villin-cre and IEC∆Chil1 mice (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by colon length measurements and H&E staining shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Upon DSS challenge, IEC∆Chil1 mice show significantly shorter colon length compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: However, upon DSS challenge, the IEC∆Chil1 mice showed significantly shorter colon length, faster body weight loss, and more severe inflammation compared to the Villin-cre mice (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by colon length measurements shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: Upon DSS challenge, IEC∆Chil1 mice show faster body weight loss compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: However, upon DSS challenge, the IEC∆Chil1 mice showed significantly shorter colon length, faster body weight loss, and more severe inflammation compared to the Villin-cre mice (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight measurements shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: Upon DSS challenge, IEC∆Chil1 mice show more severe inflammation compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: However, upon DSS challenge, the IEC∆Chil1 mice showed significantly shorter colon length, faster body weight loss, and more severe inflammation compared to the Villin-cre mice (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by H&E staining shown in Figures 5C-E.

claim: After antibiotics treatment to eliminate gut microbiota, IEC∆Chil1 mice exhibit a milder colitis phenotype compared to Villin-cre mice.
source: However, the IEC∆Chil1 mice exhibited a milder colitis phenotype, including slower body weight loss, longer colon length, and less inflammation compared to the Villin-cre mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by colitis measurements after antibiotics treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Chi3l1's effects on gut microbiota play a more significant role in colitis than its direct effects on the host.
source: Based on these findings, it is apparent that Chi3l1's effects on gut microbiota play a more significant role in colitis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that microbiota depletion reverses the colitis phenotype in IEC∆Chil1 mice.

claim: FMT from Villin-cre mice partially restores the colon length of IEC∆Chil1 mice after DSS challenge.
source: FMT partially restored the colon length of IEC∆Chil1 mice to that of Villin-cre mice after the DSS challenge, but did not have an impact on body weight loss or the level of inflammation in the gut (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by FMT experiments shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: FMT from Villin-cre mice does not impact body weight loss in IEC∆Chil1 mice after DSS challenge.
source: FMT partially restored the colon length of IEC∆Chil1 mice to that of Villin-cre mice after the DSS challenge, but did not have an impact on body weight loss or the level of inflammation in the gut (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by FMT experiments shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: FMT from Villin-cre mice does not impact the level of inflammation in IEC∆Chil1 mice after DSS challenge.
source: FMT partially restored the colon length of IEC∆Chil1 mice to that of Villin-cre mice after the DSS challenge, but did not have an impact on body weight loss or the level of inflammation in the gut (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by FMT experiments shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: IEC∆Chil1 mice transplanted with Lactobacillus display a similar colitis phenotype as Villin-cre mice.
source: IEC∆Chil1 mice transplanted with Lactobacillus displayed a similar colitis phenotype as Villin-cre mice, characterized by similar weight loss, colon length reduction, and gut inflammation (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Lactobacillus transplantation experiments shown in Figures 5G-I.

claim: Chi3l1-regulated gut microbiota, especially Lactobacillus, offers protection against colitis.
source: These findings further validate the notion that Chi3l1-regulated gut microbiota, especially Lactobacillus, offers protection against colitis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from FMT and Lactobacillus transplantation experiments showing restoration of colitis phenotype.

claim: Chi3l1 binds to bacterial PGN, helping anchor and organize bacteria within the mucus layer.
source: Our 'scaffold model' demonstrates that Chi3l1 binds to bacterial PGN, helping anchor and organize bacteria within the mucus layer.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Chi3l1 interaction with bacteria promotes the colonization of beneficial bacteria, enhancing gut health.
source: This interaction promotes the colonization of beneficial bacteria, enhancing gut health.
evidence: The claim is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Chi3l1 belongs to the glycosylhydrolase 18 family.
source: Chitinase 3-like protein 1 (Chi3l1, also known as YKL-40 in humans) is a secreted protein that belongs to the glycosylhydrolase 18 family (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2011.

claim: Chi3l1 can bind to chitin but does not have chitinase activity.
source: Despite its name, Chi3l1 can bind to chitin but does not have chitinase activity (Houston et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Houston et al., 2003.

claim: Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to cancer.
source: Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to various diseases including cancer, obesity, and neurological disorders (Bäumler and Sperandio, 2016; Charbonneau et al., 2016; Honda and Littman, 2016; Sonnenburg and Bäckhed, 2016; Thaiss et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to obesity.
source: Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to various diseases including cancer, obesity, and neurological disorders (Bäumler and Sperandio, 2016; Charbonneau et al., 2016; Honda and Littman, 2016; Sonnenburg and Bäckhed, 2016; Thaiss et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to neurological disorders.
source: Alterations in gut microbiota composition have been linked to various diseases including cancer, obesity, and neurological disorders (Bäumler and Sperandio, 2016; Charbonneau et al., 2016; Honda and Littman, 2016; Sonnenburg and Bäckhed, 2016; Thaiss et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dysbiosis is characterized by decreased microbial diversity, the presence of harmful microbes, or absence of beneficial ones.
source: Dysbiosis, which refers to an imbalance in gut microbiota, is characterized by decreased microbial diversity, the presence of harmful microbes, or absence of beneficial ones (Petersen and Round, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petersen and Round, 2014.

claim: Mouse models lacking key components of the mucus are predisposed to colitis, accompanied by dysbiosis in mucosa.
source: Although the cause of the IBD is unclear, mouse models lacking the key components of the mucus are predisposed to colitis, accompanied by dysbiosis in mucosa (Fu et al., 2011; Johansson et al., 2008), which is in accordance with increased epithelial-adherent microbial communities in biopsies from patients with IBD (Johansson et al., 2014; Swidsinski et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2011 and Johansson et al., 2008.

claim: Increased epithelial-adherent microbial communities are found in biopsies from patients with IBD.
source: Although the cause of the IBD is unclear, mouse models lacking the key components of the mucus are predisposed to colitis, accompanied by dysbiosis in mucosa (Fu et al., 2011; Johansson et al., 2008), which is in accordance with increased epithelial-adherent microbial communities in biopsies from patients with IBD (Johansson et al., 2014; Swidsinski et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Johansson et al., 2014 and Swidsinski et al., 2005.

claim: Significant differences in gut microbiota of CD patients compared with healthy controls are only present in mucus samples, not stool samples.
source: Furthermore, there were significant differences in the gut microbiota of CD patients compared with healthy controls, and these differences were only present in mucus samples (not stool samples), suggesting that bacteria in the mucus layer may be more important for the development of IBD (Gevers et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gevers et al., 2014.

claim: The intestinal flora utilizes host immunoglobulin A (IgA) for mucus colonization.
source: Donaldson et al. discovered that the intestinal flora utilizes host immunoglobulin A (IgA) for mucus colonization, indicating that the host may secrete certain factors to maintain intestinal flora homeostasis in the mucus (Donaldson et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Donaldson et al., 2018.

claim: Both live Escherichia coli and heat-killed E. coli treatment result in a significant increase in the expression of the gene encoding Chi3l1 in human intestinal organoids.
source: In a previous study, it was observed that both live Escherichia coli and heat-killed E. coli treatment resulted in a significant increase in the expression of the gene encoding Chi3l1 in human intestinal organoids (Hill et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hill et al., 2017.

claim: The gut microbiota's composition is shaped by host factors, including IgA.
source: The gut microbiota's composition is shaped by host factors, including IgA (Donaldson et al., 2018), RegIIIγ (Vaishnava et al., 2011), and TLR-5 (Fulde et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Donaldson et al., 2018.

claim: The gut microbiota's composition is shaped by host factors, including RegIIIγ.
source: The gut microbiota's composition is shaped by host factors, including IgA (Donaldson et al., 2018), RegIIIγ (Vaishnava et al., 2011), and TLR-5 (Fulde et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vaishnava et al., 2011.

claim: The gut microbiota's composition is shaped by host factors, including TLR-5.
source: The gut microbiota's composition is shaped by host factors, including IgA (Donaldson et al., 2018), RegIIIγ (Vaishnava et al., 2011), and TLR-5 (Fulde et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fulde et al., 2018.

claim: Intestinal homeostasis is crucial for maintaining human health.
source: Intestinal homeostasis is crucial for maintaining human health (Lozupone et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lozupone et al., 2012.

claim: Colonization of the gut mucus layer can affect the susceptibility and progression of intestinal diseases like inflammatory bowel disease.
source: Growing evidence suggests that colonization of the gut mucus layer can affect the susceptibility and progression of intestinal diseases like inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), irritable bowel syndrome, and celiac disease (Gordon, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gordon, 2012.

claim: Colonization of the gut mucus layer can affect the susceptibility and progression of irritable bowel syndrome.
source: Growing evidence suggests that colonization of the gut mucus layer can affect the susceptibility and progression of intestinal diseases like inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), irritable bowel syndrome, and celiac disease (Gordon, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gordon, 2012.

claim: Colonization of the gut mucus layer can affect the susceptibility and progression of celiac disease.
source: Growing evidence suggests that colonization of the gut mucus layer can affect the susceptibility and progression of intestinal diseases like inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), irritable bowel syndrome, and celiac disease (Gordon, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gordon, 2012.
